newsitem.title: GERMANY: Police out in force to guard German nuclear waste.
newsitem.headline: Police out in force to guard German nuclear waste.

text.p: Police from a 30,000-strong task force began escorting controversial nuclear waste shipments across Germany on Friday, restraining thousands of protesters in the biggest security operation in the country's post-war history.

Six containers of nuclear waste from plants in Germany and France arrived at a rail station in this southern German town on Friday and were scheduled to begin their slow journey towards a storage depot in the northern state of Lower Saxony on Monday.

The security operation will cost at least 66 million marks ($39 million) and surpass the 46 million marks spent on bringing a smaller shipment to Gorleben last year, when 19,000 police were needed to get the nuclear waste past thousands of protesters.

Shouting at police "We have friends, you don't", hundreds of demonstrators tried to thwart the trucks loaded with three 112-tonne nuclear waste containers from a power plant in Neckarwestheim to the rail station five km (three miles) away.
Helmet-clad riot police carried away demonstrators sitting in front of the plant's gates and escorted the flatbed trucks transporting the grey containers past the demonstrators.
Despite a ban on demonstrations within 50 metres of the convoy, some protesters tried to block the road by chaining themselves together. They were carried off by police.

The trucks had special metal grating to protect their tyres, headlights and windshields. Police detained more than 100 demonstrators, including four caught throwing rocks at the convoy. But the protest was mostly peaceful.
"We are glad the demonstrators are respecting the dignity of the police officers," police spokesman Peter Hetger said.

It took nearly three hours to move the containers the short distance to Walheim, where they were to be put on flatbed rail cars together with shipments from France and Bavaria which arrived later in the day.
The Lower Saxony state government has said around 30,000 police and border guards will be needed to protect the convoy on its way to the storage depot at Gorleben.

Police reported a quieter send-off for the shipment from Grundremmingen in Bavaria. A train containing one container of waste and several wagons of police guards from the plant left without major incident.
Six activists briefly held up the trucks in Neckarwestheim by forming a human chain across the street. Around 50 fellow protesters outside the police barricade shouted: "Keep it up!"
The route was guarded by dozens of police vehicles, helicopters, two water cannons and a tank.
The French shipment, from the La Hague reproccessing plant, crossed the border into Germany on Friday morning.

Protests have heated up ahead of the shipment and suspected anti-nuclear activists have sabotaged rail lines, smashed windows of public buildings in Hamburg and daubed walls with anti-nuclear slogans.
Interior Minister Manfred Kanther told parliament on Thursday he would not shrink from a test of strength if it was forced on him by the activists. ($ = 1.691 German Marks)
